subject: routing a task to the frontier reasoning tier (Claude Opus)

cases.scenario: A team's agent router sends every incoming task to the most capable model 'to be safe.' The queue includes a mix of work: a few genuinely hard architecture reviews, but mostly frontmatter edits, CSV reshaping, and status polling.
cases.context: Production agent fleet on a metered budget; latency and per-token cost both matter; the team frames the smartest model as the low-risk default.
cases.question: Evaluate this routing policy and recommend what to change.
expected_flags: Defaulting every task to the frontier tier is the wrong default — it over-pays on the majority of tasks a cheaper tier clears identically and starves budget for the genuinely hard work
Under uncertainty routing should move DOWN until a task proves it needs the ceiling, not UP
The mechanical work (frontmatter edits, CSV reshaping, polling) belongs on the fast tier or a script, not the frontier tier
expected_fix_hints: Make the default lane the balanced tier and escalate to the frontier tier only on a named difficulty signal
Route the mechanical/high-volume items to the fast tier or to a deterministic script
absent_signals: Do not endorse 'smartest model when in doubt' as a safe default
Do not claim the frontier tier adds quality on mechanical work

cases.scenario: A payment-reconciliation job intermittently double-counts a small fraction of orders. It reproduces only under concurrent load, spans three services and two database views, and a prior single-pass attempt on a cheaper tier declared it fixed after one clean run — the bug recurred in production.
cases.context: The cost of a wrong reconciliation is financial; the failure is non-deterministic and multi-system.
cases.question: Which model tier should investigate this, and why?
expected_flags: This is intermittent, multi-system root-cause work — a difficulty signal that earns the frontier tier
A cheaper tier's tendency to declare it fixed after one clean run is exactly the failure mode the frontier tier guards against here
High cost-of-error (financial miscalculation) reinforces escalation
expected_fix_hints: Route the investigation to the frontier reasoning tier
Give the full multi-service context up front so the model can hold it coherently
absent_signals: Do not route intermittent multi-system root-cause to a cheaper tier to save cost
Do not accept a single clean run as proof the bug is fixed

cases.scenario: An engineer asks the frontier tier to rename a SCSS class across 8 files and update the imports, reasoning that the change touches many files so it must be a 'multi-file' task that needs the smartest model.
cases.context: The rename is a deterministic find-and-replace with a known target string; no judgment is required.
cases.question: Is the frontier tier the right executor here? Justify.
expected_flags: Touching many files is not the same as multi-file SYNTHESIS — a deterministic bulk rename needs no reasoning ceiling
This is script-grade work; even the fast tier is unnecessary
The 'multi-file' signal that earns the frontier tier is correctness depending on holding many files in working context, not the raw file count
expected_fix_hints: Use a deterministic script (sed/codemod) for the rename and import update
If a model is wanted for safety review of the diff, the fast tier suffices
absent_signals: Do not equate high file count with a need for the frontier reasoning tier
Do not route a deterministic find-and-replace to any premium model

cases.scenario: A team wants an overnight agentic run that refactors a subsystem across many modules, must stay coherent over dozens of steps without human correction, and will not be reviewed until morning.
cases.context: No human is in the loop during the run; drift or incoherence mid-run is expensive to unwind.
cases.question: How should the agent be configured for this run — which tier and what effort posture?
expected_flags: Long-horizon autonomous work that must stay coherent without human correction is a frontier-tier signal
The full task spec should be given up front in one turn so the model can plan the whole horizon
Run at high/xhigh effort — the effort ceiling the frontier tier alone provides is the point
expected_fix_hints: Route to the frontier tier and supply the complete spec in the first turn
Set effort to high or xhigh; consider task budgets to cap autonomous spend
absent_signals: Do not assume a cheaper tier will stay coherent over a long unsupervised horizon
Do not drip-feed the spec turn-by-turn for a long autonomous run

cases.scenario: A reviewer argues against using the frontier tier for a large multi-file task, saying 'the 1M context window makes it too expensive to feed big inputs, so send big tasks to a cheaper model to save money.'
cases.context: The decision rests on a pricing claim about long-context behavior on the current frontier generation.
cases.question: Assess the reviewer's reasoning.
expected_flags: The wide window does not itself carry a long-context per-token premium on the current frontier generation, so 'big inputs make it too expensive' is a false premise
Routing big multi-file SYNTHESIS to a cheaper tier to save token cost risks wrong answers, the more expensive outcome
Any pricing/context claim should be verified live against the provider's docs, not asserted from memory
expected_fix_hints: Correct the premise: the 1M window is not itself a cost reason to avoid the frontier tier
Decide on task difficulty (does it need the reasoning ceiling), then verify the pricing fact live
absent_signals: Do not accept that the wide context window carries a long-context pricing premium on the current generation
Do not route hard synthesis down purely on an unverified cost claim

cases.scenario: A task is fully specified: add a paginated list endpoint following an existing controller pattern in the repo, with tests, against a well-understood codebase. The author wants to use the frontier tier 'because it's an important feature.'
cases.context: The pattern to follow already exists; the work is ordinary, well-specified implementation.
cases.question: Which tier fits, and what is the test for the decision?
expected_flags: Importance is not a difficulty signal — ordinary well-specified feature work clears the balanced tier
The escalation test is 'would the balanced tier plausibly get this wrong,' and here the answer is no
Paying the frontier premium here buys nothing over the balanced tier
expected_fix_hints: Route to the balanced tier (claude-sonnet) for well-specified feature work plus tests
Reserve the frontier tier for a named difficulty signal, not for 'this matters'
absent_signals: Do not treat task importance as a reason to escalate to the frontier tier
Do not pay the frontier premium for work the balanced tier clears reliably

cases.scenario: A team asks two things at once: (a) design the supervisor-and-checkpoint loop topology their overnight agent will run inside, and (b) write the Anthropic Messages API request that sets the thinking config and effort for that agent. They frame both as 'Opus questions.'
cases.context: The loop topology and the API call syntax are separate concerns from which model tier to pick; the team folds them under the Opus label.
cases.question: How should the agent scope and route this request?
expected_flags: Designing the supervisor/checkpoint loop is loop architecture (autonomous-loop-patterns), not a model-tier decision
Writing the Messages API request with thinking/effort config is call-site syntax (the claude-api reference), not the routing decision
Neither sub-question is answered by the frontier-tier routing skill; both should be redirected to their owners
expected_fix_hints: Route the loop-topology design to autonomous-loop-patterns
Route the API request syntax to the claude-api reference
absent_signals: Do not answer loop-topology design as if it were a model-tier choice
Do not write the API request syntax under the frontier-tier routing skill's lane
